stem: A container app loads a 4 GB model into memory before it can serve anything, which takes about three minutes. It keeps being restarted during that window. Which probe should be configured to fix this?

options.text: A startup probe, run during the startup phase
A liveness probe with a longer period
A readiness probe with a higher success threshold
No probe; disable ingress until the model loads

explanation: The startup probe exists precisely for the slow-boot case: it is checked separately from liveness during the initial startup phase, so a container that is still loading is not judged dead. Its default failure threshold of 240 with a one-second period gives a generous window to widen further.

whyWrong.B: A longer period just spaces out the failing checks; the app still fails them and is still restarted.
whyWrong.C: Readiness governs whether traffic is routed, not whether the replica is killed.
whyWrong.D: Ingress is not something you toggle per-startup, and the restarts would continue regardless.

docs.title: Health probes in Azure Container Apps

hint: One of the three probe types is defined as running only during the initial startup phase.

stem: A container app runs in multiple revision mode. A new revision is deployed, and traffic must not reach it until its replicas can actually serve requests. What governs that?

options.text: The readiness probe, before shifting traffic
The liveness probe, once the replica is not restarting
The startup probe, once startup completes
The provisioning state, once it reaches Provisioned

explanation: Readiness is the probe that answers "can this replica handle incoming requests". In single revision mode Container Apps shifts traffic automatically once readiness succeeds; in multiple revision mode you control the split yourself, so it is on you to wait for readiness before moving the weights.

whyWrong.B: Liveness only says the process is still alive and responsive, which is a weaker claim than being able to serve.
whyWrong.C: Startup finishing means the app booted, not that dependencies are reachable.
whyWrong.D: A provisioned revision can still have replicas that are not ready.

docs.title: Health probes in Azure Container Apps

stem: Which two statements about Azure Container Apps health probes are true? Choose two.

options.text: You can define at most one probe of each type per container
`exec` probes, which run a command inside the container, are not supported
Probes can target a named port defined in the container spec
gRPC probes are supported in addition to HTTP and TCP
A failing liveness probe takes the replica out of rotation without restarting it

explanation: Container Apps supports HTTP(S) and TCP probes only, one of each type per container, and does not support `exec` or gRPC. Ports must be integers — named ports are not supported. An HTTP probe succeeds on a status code of at least 200 and below 400.

whyWrong.C: Named ports are explicitly unsupported; port values must be integers.
whyWrong.D: gRPC probes are on the unsupported list alongside `exec`.
whyWrong.E: That describes readiness. Liveness failure means the replica is restarted.

docs.title: Health probes in Azure Container Apps — Restrictions

stem: A container app has ingress enabled and no probes defined in its template. A sidecar container was added alongside the main container. What is true about probes on this app?

options.text: The main container gets defaults; the sidecar gets none
Both containers get default TCP probes on the ingress target port
Neither container gets probes, because none were defined in the template
Both containers get default HTTP probes against `/health`

explanation: When ingress is enabled the portal fills in default startup, liveness and readiness probes on the main app container — TCP, against the ingress target port — for each type you did not define yourself. Sidecars are left alone, so a sidecar that needs a probe needs one written explicitly.

whyWrong.B: Defaults are not added to sidecar containers.
whyWrong.C: The defaults are added for you; assuming no probes exist is how people are surprised by restarts.
whyWrong.D: The defaults are TCP, not HTTP, and there is no assumed `/health` path.

docs.title: Health probes in Azure Container Apps — Default configuration

hint: The defaults are attached to one specific container, and they use the simplest protocol available.

stem: Complete the probe definition so that the runtime restarts the replica when the app stops responding, checking an HTTP endpoint.
code:
probes:
  - type: [1]
    [2]:
      path: "/health"
      port: 8080
    initialDelaySeconds: 7
    periodSeconds: 3

blanks.label: Blank 1 — the probe type that triggers a restart

explanation: Liveness is the probe whose failure means the replica is restarted; readiness only removes it from rotation. The HTTP mechanism is `httpGet` — `tcpSocket` would ignore the path, and `exec` is not supported in Container Apps at all.

docs.title: Health probes in Azure Container Apps

stem: One replica out of six in a revision is repeatedly failing its readiness probe. How does Container Apps report and handle this?

options.text: The revision shows unhealthy and the replica is restarted
The revision stays healthy because most replicas pass
The revision is deactivated and traffic fails back
The replica stays in rotation with a degraded header

explanation: Revision health is not a majority vote: one failing replica marks the revision unhealthy even when the other five are fine. Container Apps keeps restarting the offending replica until it passes or blows through the failure threshold — at which point the revision is usually misconfigured rather than unlucky.

whyWrong.B: There is no quorum rule; a single failing replica is enough to show the revision as unhealthy.
whyWrong.C: Automatic failover to a previous revision is not what happens — traffic weights are yours to manage.
whyWrong.D: Nothing decorates responses; an unready replica does not receive traffic.

docs.title: Health probes in Azure Container Apps — Default configuration

stem: An inference API on Container Apps is configured with `minReplicas: 0`. Users report that the first request after a quiet period takes several seconds, while later requests are fast. What is the trade-off being made?

options.text: Scaling to zero removes billing for idle time at the cost of a cold start on the first request
Scaling to zero disables the readiness probe, so the first request arrives before the app is ready
Scaling to zero forces the revision into single revision mode, which serialises requests
Scaling to zero switches the app to the consumption profile, which throttles the first request

explanation: `minReplicas: 0` is the scale-to-zero setting: with no replicas running you pay nothing for idle, but the next request has to wait for a replica to be created, the image to start and the app to become ready. Setting `minReplicas: 1` buys away the cold start by keeping one replica warm.

whyWrong.B: Probes still run on the new replica — the delay is the replica being created, not a probe being skipped.
whyWrong.C: Revision mode is an independent setting and does not serialise requests.
whyWrong.D: Workload profile is chosen separately, and nothing throttles the first request.

docs.title: Set scaling rules in Azure Container Apps

hint: Nothing is broken. Ask what has to happen between the request arriving and a replica existing.

stem: A validated image already exists in a development Azure Container Registry and must be copied into the production registry without rebuilding it and without pulling it to a local machine. Which command does this?

options.text: `az acr import --name prodacr --source devacr.azurecr.io/copilot:v3 --image copilot:v3`
`az acr build --registry prodacr --image copilot:v3 .`
`az acr repository update --name prodacr --image copilot:v3`
`docker tag devacr.azurecr.io/copilot:v3 prodacr.azurecr.io/copilot:v3 && docker push prodacr.azurecr.io/copilot:v3`

explanation: `az acr import` copies an image registry-to-registry on the service side. Nothing is pulled locally and nothing is rebuilt, so the digest that was tested in dev is the digest that lands in production — which is the point of promoting rather than rebuilding.

whyWrong.B: `az acr build` produces a new image from source; the artefact you tested is not the one you ship.
whyWrong.C: `az acr repository update` changes attributes such as write-enabled; it does not copy images.
whyWrong.D: This works but violates the constraint — it pulls to and pushes from the local machine, and needs a Docker daemon.

docs.title: Import container images to a container registry

stem: A container app should be reachable only from other apps in the same Container Apps environment, never from the internet, while still being addressable by name over HTTP. How should ingress be configured?

options.text: Ingress enabled with external traffic set to internal, so the app gets an environment-internal FQDN
Ingress disabled, and callers reach it by replica IP address
Ingress enabled and external, protected by an IP restriction list covering the environment's subnet
Ingress enabled and external, with authentication required on every route

explanation: Internal ingress gives the app a stable FQDN that resolves only inside the environment. The alternatives either give up name-based addressing or expose a public endpoint and then try to fence it off, which is more moving parts for a weaker guarantee.

whyWrong.B: With ingress disabled there is no endpoint or FQDN, and replica IPs are not stable.
whyWrong.C: The endpoint is still public; an IP allowlist is a filter in front of exposure, not the absence of it.
whyWrong.D: Authentication protects the endpoint but does not stop it being internet-reachable.
